title: Future Forms Fair
intro: Will, going to, the present continuous or the present simple? Pick the future that fits the situation.

A2.q: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
A2.why: You can see the clouds now: evidence, so “going to”, and it needs “is”.

A2.q: I ___ call you tonight, I promise.
A2.why: A promise made now: will + verb.
“Every day” is a timetable: present simple.

A2.q: We ___ to the cinema tonight — I’ve already bought the tickets.
A2.why: The tickets are bought, so it’s arranged: present continuous, not “go” as in Spanish “vamos”.

A2.q: I think it ___ be sunny tomorrow.
A2.why: “I think” plus an opinion about the future: will.
You can see it about to happen: “are going to”, with the “are”.
A fixed arrangement with a time: present continuous (am meeting).
“On weekdays” is a timetable: present simple.

A2.q: I'm thirsty. I ___ get a glass of water.
A2.why: A decision made at the moment of speaking: will + verb.

A2.q: She ___ having a party next Saturday — she's already invited everyone.
A2.why: Everyone is invited, so it’s arranged: present continuous (is having).

A2.q: I’ll phone you when I ___ to the hotel.
A2.why: After “when” about the future, English uses the present simple.

A2.q: The bus to the Albufera ___ at ten o’clock tomorrow morning.
A2.why: A bus timetable: present simple with -s, even for tomorrow.

B1.q: By the time you arrive, I ___ finished cooking.
B1.why: “By the time you arrive” looks back from a future point: future perfect.
A fixed schedule: present simple with -s, even for “next Monday”.

B1.q: I promise I ___ help you tomorrow.
B1.why: “I promise” goes with will, not the present as in Spanish “te ayudo”.

B1.q: Look at the sky — it ___ to rain any minute.
B1.why: Look at the sky: evidence now, so “is going to rain”.

B1.q: We ___ to Italy next summer — the flights are already booked.
B1.why: The flights are booked: an arrangement, so present continuous.

B1.q: This time next week, I ___ lying on a beach.
B1.why: “This time next week” plus an action in progress: future continuous.

B1.q: The plane ___ at 7:45, so we need to leave now.
B1.why: Flights run to a timetable: present simple, and it hasn’t left yet.
A promise about the future: will; the present “call” is the Spanish “te llamo”.

B1.q: She’s studying really hard — she ___ pass the exam.
B1.why: Evidence now (she’s studying hard) points to the result: “is going to”.

B1.q: By next year, they ___ married for a decade.
B1.why: “By next year” plus a length of time up to then: future perfect.

B1.q: We’ll start the paella as soon as Grandma ___ .
B1.why: After “as soon as” about the future: present simple.

B1.q: The sheriff ___ the new deputy at noon tomorrow — it’s all arranged.
B1.why: “It’s all arranged” with a time: present continuous.

B2.q: By 2030, scientists ___ found a cure, according to experts.
B2.why: “By 2030” looks back from a future point: future perfect.

B2.q: This time tomorrow, we ___ flying over the Atlantic.
B2.why: “This time tomorrow” plus an action in progress: future continuous.

B2.q: The conference ___ place next month, as scheduled.
B2.why: “As scheduled” is a timetable: present simple, even for next month.

B2.q: I can't come — I ___ working late that evening.
B2.why: An action in progress at a future time (“that evening”): future continuous.

B2.q: Given the current trend, unemployment ___ rise further.
B2.why: “Given the current trend” is evidence now: “is going to”.

B2.q: By the end of this course, you ___ mastered all the tenses.
B2.why: “By the end of this course” looks back from a future point: future perfect.

B2.q: The ceremony ___ at exactly noon tomorrow.
B2.why: A fixed programme: present simple, even for tomorrow.
“Watch out” — you can see it happening: “is going to”.

B2.q: I ___ seeing the doctor at 3pm, so I can't make the meeting.
B2.why: A fixed appointment with a time: present continuous (am seeing).

B2.q: By this time next month, she ___ her new job for six weeks.
B2.why: “By this time next month” plus “for six weeks”: future perfect.

B2.q: By the time the doctor arrives, the patient ___ for three hours.
B2.why: “By the time” plus a length of time up to a future point: future perfect continuous.

B2.q: I’ll lend you my saddle, as long as you ___ it back by Friday.
B2.why: After “as long as” about the future: present simple.

C1.q: The board ___ at 9am sharp tomorrow, as stated in the agenda.
C1.why: “As stated in the agenda” is a timetable: present simple.

C1.q: By the time the report is published, the situation ___ changed entirely.
C1.why: “By the time the report is published” looks back from the future: future perfect.

C1.q: Given current projections, the deficit ___ widen further.
C1.why: “Given current projections” is evidence now: “is going to”.

C1.q: The ambassador ___ address parliament tomorrow morning.
C1.why: A formal announcement of a future event: will + bare verb, with no “to”.

C1.q: This time next year, the company ___ operating in twelve countries.
C1.why: “This time next year” plus an ongoing activity: future continuous.

C1.q: The exhibition ___ on the 3rd of next month, as announced.
C1.why: “As announced” is a timetable: present simple for a future date.

C1.q: By the time you read this, I ___ already left.
C1.why: “By the time you read this” looks back from the future: future perfect.

C1.q: Judging by the clouds, we ___ a storm tonight.
C1.why: “Judging by the clouds” is evidence now: going to.

C1.q: The committee ___ its findings by Friday, according to the schedule.
C1.why: “By Friday” looks back from a future deadline: will have + past participle.

C1.q: By 2050, renewable energy ___ overtaken fossil fuels, most analysts agree.
C1.why: “By 2050” looks back from a future point: future perfect, and “will” is always followed by “have”.

C1.q: The new metro line ___ to open next spring, the council has announced.
C1.why: “Is due to” is for an official timetable; “about to” is only for the next few moments.

C1.q: Once the vaccine ___ approved, doctors will start giving it to the elderly.
C1.why: After “once” about the future, no “will”: present perfect for something completed first.
